strengths: Introduces FrameOracle-41K, the first large-scale VideoQA dataset providing explicit keyframe annotations (minimal sufficient frame indices and counts), which fills a genuine gap since prior datasets provide only answer-level supervision, forcing keyframe selectors to rely on weak proxies.

The four-stage curriculum is a sensible design that progressively moves from weak proxy signals (SigLIP similarity, leave-one-out loss) to strong ground-truth supervision, and the ablation in Table 4 clearly shows each stage contributes incremental value.

The dual Rank Head / K Head architecture directly addresses the practically important but under-explored problem of jointly deciding 'which frames' and 'how many frames,' distinguishing it from fixed-budget or single-model co-trained selectors.

Broad empirical validation across five VLM backbones (including a proprietary model, GPT-4o) and six diverse benchmarks (both short- and long-video) demonstrates the plug-and-play, model-agnostic nature of the method without requiring co-training.
Concrete efficiency analysis (Table 3) quantifying FLOPs, latency, and token reduction alongside accuracy gives a practically meaningful picture of the efficiency-accuracy trade-off.
Comparison against both jointly-trained (Table 2, category 1) and plug-and-play (Table 2, category 2) SOTA keyframe selectors situates the contribution well within the existing literature.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the FrameOracle-41K construction pipeline: the mining agent and the three verifier VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B, LLaVA-OneVision-72B, LLaVA-Video-72B) are from the same model families later used as backbones/supervision signals in Stages 2-3 and evaluation, raising concern that the 'minimal sufficient frame set' labels may be biased toward what these specific model families find sufficient rather than reflecting a model-agnostic notion of minimality.

Source videos for FrameOracle-41K are restricted to 2-3 minute clips from a single source corpus (LLaVA-Video-178K), yet the method is evaluated on benchmarks with much longer videos (EgoSchema, MLVU, Video-MME, some spanning many minutes to hours), creating a domain/duration mismatch between the Stage-4 supervision and the deployment setting that is not directly addressed or ablated.

Reported accuracy gains are often small and inconsistent across benchmarks (e.g., LongVideoBench accuracy sometimes decreases when moving from 16 to ~10.4 frames; Video-MME slightly declines with Stage 4 fine-tuning in Table 4), and no variance/statistical significance is reported across runs, making it hard to assess robustness of the reported improvements.

In the head-to-head comparison with other plug-and-play selectors (Table 2), FrameOracle's K Head is disabled and a fixed top-8 is used, so the paper never demonstrates its distinguishing adaptive-K capability against these directly comparable baselines, weakening the evidence for the paper's central claim of adaptive frame-count selection being superior.

The 64-frame K Head variant is explicitly capped at a maximum predicted K of 16 during Stage 3 training for comparability, which somewhat undercuts the claimed benefit of fully adaptive frame-count prediction and is a design compromise not thoroughly discussed.

The costly data-generation pipeline (iterative 72B-parameter agent exploration plus three 72B-parameter verifier models per instance) is described only qualitatively; total computational/monetary cost of building FrameOracle-41K is not reported, which is relevant for assessing practical reproducibility of the dataset creation process by other groups.

Some architectural and hyperparameter choices (e.g., single visual encoder DINOv2, single tokenizer choice, threshold λ for filtering in Stage II) are not ablated or their exact values not given in the main text, limiting insight into sensitivity of results to these design choices.

strengths: Introduces FrameOracle-41K, the first VideoQA dataset with explicit keyframe/minimal-frame annotations, which could be a useful resource for the community if released with sufficient quality control.
Extensive empirical evaluation spanning five VLM backbones (including GPT-4o) and six benchmarks (both short- and long-video), plus efficiency measurements (FLOPs, latency, token counts).
The plug-and-play, model-agnostic design (no co-training with the backbone VLM) is a practically appealing property compared to prior jointly-trained selectors.
Reasonably thorough ablation over the four training stages (Table 4) attempting to isolate the contribution of each supervision signal.
The dual Rank/K-head design tackling both 'what to see' and 'how much to see' jointly is a sensible framing of an under-addressed problem.
weaknesses: Circularity in dataset construction: the keyframe-mining agent and one of the three verifying VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) come from the same model family that is also used as the supervision backbone in Stages 2–3 of FrameOracle training, and is one of the five backbones used to report main results (Table 1). This raises concerns that the 'minimal sufficient frame' annotations and downstream gains are partly an artifact of Qwen model biases rather than a general property of video evidence.

The verification protocol ('3 VLMs answer correctly using only the keyframes') does not establish true minimality (i.e., it never checks that removing any further frame breaks correctness), and for open-ended/free-form QA sourced from LLaVA-Video-178K, correct answers can sometimes be produced via language priors/guessing rather than genuine visual grounding, which is not controlled for.

Reported accuracy gains are frequently very small (often <1 point, e.g., many entries in Table 1), and no error bars, variance across seeds, or significance tests are provided anywhere in the paper, making it hard to distinguish real improvements from noise, especially given known evaluation variance on MCQ-style video benchmarks.

Stage 1 of the curriculum (SigLIP-distillation) actually degrades performance relative to the random-selection baseline on several benchmarks (e.g., Perception 65.0→60.3, LVB 52.9→49.8 in Table 4), yet is still framed as a 'foundational' stage; the paper does not adequately justify why this stage is retained or ablate whether skipping it directly to Stage 2 yields better results.

Comparisons in Table 2 mix different sampling regimes (1fps vs. fixed uniform sampling, differing candidate pool sizes) across baselines, making the head-to-head comparison less controlled; FrameOracle also underperforms the heuristic KFC baseline on MLVU with only a post-hoc explanation rather than deeper analysis.

Key hyperparameters (e.g., relevance threshold λ in Stage II filtering, λk in Eq. 2, α in Eq. 3) are stated but not ablated or sensitivity-tested, leaving it unclear how robust the method is to these choices.

Architectural details of FrameOracle itself (number of Transformer encoder/decoder layers, hidden dimensions, parameter count) are not specified in the main text or appendix, limiting exact reproducibility despite the reproducibility statement's claims.

The dataset is derived entirely from LLaVA-Video-178K videos with similar instructional/activity content; there is no evaluation of how well FrameOracle-41K-trained selectors generalize to substantially different video domains (e.g., cinematic, egocentric, surveillance) beyond the benchmarks already sharing similar distributions.
The RQ1 finding that 'more frames don't always help' is a restatement of prior work already cited in the paper (e.g., Park et al., 2024) rather than a novel empirical contribution.

Cost and reproducibility of the expensive agent-based data generation pipeline (iterative Qwen2.5-VL-72B API calls plus three-way cross-verification) are not quantified (e.g., total API cost, wall-clock time), which may hinder independent reproduction of FrameOracle-41K.

strengths: Introduces FrameOracle-41K, the first large-scale VideoQA dataset with explicit keyframe annotations specifying minimal sufficient frame sets—this is a genuinely novel and potentially valuable resource for the community, filling a real gap since prior datasets provide only answer-level or coarse span-level supervision.

The four-stage curriculum training design (weak proxy signals → LOO-based supervision → K-head optimization → strong ground-truth SFT) is a sensible and well-motivated progression, and the ablation in Table 4 clearly demonstrates the incremental value of each stage.

Extensive empirical validation across five diverse VLM backbones (including a proprietary model, GPT-4o) and six benchmarks spanning both short- and long-video understanding, supporting the claim of plug-and-play generalizability without backbone co-training.
Efficiency analysis (Table 3) with FLOPs, latency, and token counts provides a concrete, practically relevant picture of the computational savings, not just accuracy numbers.
Good comparison against both jointly-trained (non-portable) and plug-and-play SOTA keyframe selection baselines (Table 2), situating the contribution clearly relative to prior art.
Reasonably thorough reproducibility details, including hyperparameters, training durations, dataset composition per stage, and prompt templates for the data-generation pipeline in the appendix.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in dataset construction and evaluation: the keyframe annotations in FrameOracle-41K are generated and verified entirely by VLMs from the same model families (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, LLaVA-Video) that are later used as downstream backbones in the main experiments (Table 1). This raises concern that reported gains may partly reflect distributional alignment between the labeling models and the evaluated models rather than a general improvement in keyframe selection quality.

No human verification or spot-checking of the automatically generated keyframe annotations is reported; correctness of the dataset rests solely on agreement among a small set of VLMs, which could propagate shared biases or blind spots rather than true minimal-evidence identification.

No variance/error bars or multiple random seeds are reported for any of the main results, making it hard to assess whether reported accuracy differences (often within 0.5-1.5 points) are statistically meaningful versus noise.

Several results in Table 1 and Table 2 are missing (dashes) for many model-benchmark combinations, weakening the completeness of the cross-model comparison and making some conclusions harder to verify systematically.

Key implementation details are missing or underspecified, e.g., the relevance-score filtering threshold λ in Stage II of dataset construction is never given a concrete value, and the rationale for capping K at 16 for the 64-frame selector in Stage 3 is not well justified beyond convenience for comparison.

The dataset's source videos are restricted to 2-3 minute clips from LLaVA-Video-178K; it is unclear how well FrameOracle transfers to much longer videos (e.g., hour-long content in HourVideo-style settings) despite being evaluated on long-video benchmarks.
On MLVU, FrameOracle underperforms a simpler heuristic (KFC), and the paper's explanation for this gap is somewhat post-hoc without deeper analysis or mitigation.

Overall accuracy improvements are often modest in absolute terms (frequently under 1-2 points), so the core value proposition rests more on efficiency gains than on accuracy gains, which is reasonable but could be stated more precisely/cautiously in the abstract and conclusion.

strengths: Introduces FrameOracle-41K, the first large-scale VideoQA dataset with explicit minimal-keyframe annotations; construction pipeline is described in detail and validated with a substantial human study (4,000 samples, 94% inter-annotator agreement, 93.3% verified accuracy, and a sufficiency-classification analysis showing 96.7% of samples are 'just-right').

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 5 VLM backbones, 6 benchmarks, comparisons against both jointly-trained and plug-and-play SOTA keyframe selectors, plus FLOPs/latency/token accounting and statistical significance testing via bootstrap confidence intervals.

Thoughtful ablation studies (Appendix F) addressing many natural questions: necessity of the 4-stage curriculum, sensitivity to the supervision-backbone choice, whether gains stem from frame selection vs. mere frame reduction, frame-level vs. token-level budgeting, and comparison to memory-compression baselines — this breadth substantially strengthens the soundness of the core claims.
The method is architecturally simple, lightweight, and genuinely plug-and-play/backbone-agnostic, which is a practically valuable property compared to co-training approaches cited in related work.
Reasonably good reproducibility: hyperparameters, training times, dataset JSON format, and prompts for data generation are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in the dataset construction/verification process: 'ground-truth' minimal keyframes are defined operationally by whether Qwen2.5-VL-72B (mining agent) and three large VLMs (verification) can answer correctly using them. This risks biasing the notion of 'minimal sufficiency' toward frame subsets that happen to be easy for a narrow family of large transformer-based VLMs, rather than a model-independent semantic ground truth; the paper does not discuss or test this potential bias (e.g., via a different model family for verification).

The headline accuracy improvements are modest (avg. +1.5% at 64-frame candidates, no loss at 16-frame candidates), and several individual benchmark deltas in Table 1 are flagged as not statistically significant (§), somewhat tempering the significance of the accuracy claims (though the efficiency gains are more convincingly substantiated).

The K-Head target (Eq. 2) depends on a hand-tuned linear penalty λk that trades off accuracy and frame count; sensitivity of results to this hyperparameter is not analyzed, and the appropriateness of the accuracy/efficiency trade-off point chosen is not well justified beyond the reported empirical outcome.

The MLVU results show FrameOracle underperforming some SOTA baselines at matched candidate pools, requiring an ad hoc segment-wise inference-time patch (Appendix F.4) to remain competitive on very long videos — this suggests limited generalization of the trained fixed-size selector to substantially longer/denser videos without manual reconfiguration.

Comparisons in Table 2 mix differing candidate pool sizes across methods (e.g., FrameOracle 64→8 vs. competitors using 1fps or 128/256 frame pools), which, while disclosed, complicates a fully apples-to-apples efficiency comparison.

The Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate non-statement, providing no substantive discussion of limitations or ethical/societal considerations (e.g., reliance on proprietary/large VLM APIs for dataset construction, potential biases inherited from LLaVA-Video-178K source data).

strengths: Introduces FrameOracle-41K, which to the authors' knowledge is the first VideoQA dataset with explicit keyframe-level (minimal sufficient frame) annotations, filling a real gap in supervision for frame selection research.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning five VLM backbones and six benchmarks, with paired bootstrap significance testing reported for most comparisons, which is more rigorous than many papers in this space.

Thorough ablation suite (Appendix F) examining the necessity of the multi-stage curriculum, sensitivity to the supervision backbone, frame-level vs. token-level budgeting, segment-wise extension for long videos, and comparison against memory-compression baselines, which collectively support several of the design choices.

The method is plug-and-play and backbone-agnostic, requiring no co-training with the downstream VLM, which is a practically appealing property relative to several cited baselines that require joint training.
Reports concrete efficiency metrics (FLOPs, latency, token counts) in addition to accuracy, giving a more complete picture of the efficiency-accuracy trade-off than accuracy-only comparisons.
weaknesses: Potential circularity in dataset construction and evaluation: FrameOracle-41K's keyframe annotations are validated by requiring Qwen2.5-VL-72B, LLaVA-OneVision-72B, and LLaVA-Video-72B to answer correctly using only the mined keyframes, while the main experiments subsequently evaluate FrameOracle (trained partly on this dataset) on backbones from the exact same model families (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-Video, LLaVA-OneVision). This risks a biased 'ground truth' that favors frames these specific model families find sufficient, inflating apparent gains for related backbones and raising questions about generalization to unrelated architectures (e.g., proprietary models not from these families).

The claim of 'minimal sufficient' frames is only loosely validated: the human verification tolerance for 'just-right' is ±3 frames, which is a large relative margin given a reported median of 5 frames (up to 60%+ deviation), so the 96.7% 'just-right' statistic overstates precision of the minimality claim.

The Stage 2/3 training relies on leave-one-out VLM loss computation for every candidate frame per sample to generate soft supervision signals, which is computationally expensive at scale (N forward passes per training example); this cost is not quantified or discussed, raising reproducibility and scalability concerns.

Several reported gains are modest or statistically non-significant (marked § in Table 1), and the headline '1.5% average improvement' partly rests on a few larger gains rather than uniformly significant improvements across all benchmarks/backbones.

The predicted K is arbitrarily capped at 16 in the 64-frame setting for 'comparability,' which undercuts the paper's central claim of adaptively deciding 'how much to see,' since the dynamic budget is externally constrained in the very setting meant to showcase larger-pool adaptivity.

The Impact Statement is entirely generic boilerplate with no substantive discussion of limitations, potential biases introduced by the automated agent-based annotation pipeline, or risks of using LLM/VLM-generated supervision signals as ground truth; limitations in the main text are confined to a brief forward-looking remark in the conclusion.

Fairness of some baseline comparisons is questionable (e.g., reporting Qwen baselines at 32/128 frames due to internal frame-merging to match 'raw frame' counts of other models), which complicates direct comparison and may understate or overstate relative efficiency depending on interpretation.

The architecture introduces an additional visual encoder (DINOv2) separate from the downstream VLM's own vision encoder, adding pipeline complexity and potential representational mismatch that is not analyzed.

strengths: Introduces FrameOracle-41K, the first large-scale VideoQA dataset with explicit minimal-sufficient-keyframe annotations, built via a well-documented two-stage agent-mining + multi-VLM verification pipeline, with a credible human verification study (94% inter-annotator agreement, 93.3% verified accuracy, and a 'minimal sufficiency' check showing 96.7% of samples are 'just-right').

The proposed architecture (cross-modal fusion encoder + dual Rank/K heads) is simple, lightweight, and genuinely backbone-agnostic, addressing a clearly articulated gap (fixed-budget vs. adaptive selection, backbone co-training vs. plug-and-play).

Extensive empirical evaluation across five VLM backbones and six benchmarks (both long- and short-video), with statistically validated gains (bootstrap CIs) and consistent efficiency-accuracy trade-offs (e.g., 16→10.4 frames with no accuracy loss, 64→13.9 with +1.5% accuracy).

Rich set of ablations (Appendix F) rigorously justify design choices: necessity of the 4-stage curriculum (joint training destabilizes optimization, Kendall-tau drops from 0.54 to 0.23), robustness to different supervision backbones, disentangling 'fewer frames' from 'better frames' via equal-budget comparison, frame-level vs. token-level budgeting, and comparison with memory-compression baselines.

Favorable comparisons against a wide range of recent SOTA keyframe-selection methods (jointly-trained and plug-and-play), including compute/latency/token accounting (Table 3) that transparently shows FrameOracle's own overhead is small relative to VLM cost.
Clear writing and good contextualization of related work distinguishing agent-based, co-trained, and heuristic adaptive selection approaches.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/bias in dataset construction and training supervision: both the FrameOracle-41K ground-truth mining (Qwen2.5-VL-72B agent, verification by Qwen2.5-VL-72B/LLaVA-OneVision-72B/LLaVA-Video-72B) and the weak-supervision training stages (Qwen2.5-VL-3B as backbone for LOO signals) draw heavily from the same model families used later for evaluation, raising questions about whether 'minimal sufficiency' reflects genuine human-perceivable evidence versus idiosyncrasies of these specific VLMs; the human verification, while reassuring, covers only ~10% of the dataset.

FrameOracle does not consistently beat all SOTA methods on MLVU with a 64-frame pool (acknowledged by the authors), and the proposed segment-wise fix is only validated in a limited follow-up ablation rather than integrated into the main pipeline/results.

The method pipeline is fairly complex (4 training stages, multiple heads, several loss terms and hyperparameters such as λ, λk, α), with long cumulative training times (up to ~190 GPU-hours per variant across stages on 8×H100s); sensitivity of key hyperparameters (e.g., the Stage II relevance threshold λ, the frame-cost penalty λk) is not analyzed.
Some comparison tables (e.g., Table 2) contain missing entries for several baselines/benchmarks, making head-to-head conclusions in RQ2 only partially complete.

Generalization beyond the 2–3 minute video regime used to build FrameOracle-41K is not directly tested with annotated data; evidence for very long videos (hours) relies on an inference-time segment-wise heuristic rather than on dataset-level supervision for such durations.

Limited discussion of failure modes, dataset bias inherited from the source corpus (LLaVA-Video-178K), and broader limitations/ethical considerations (the Impact Statement is essentially a boilerplate with no substantive discussion).
